I have been getting great suggestions from people both PMing and posting. Thank you to all the Goats out there that are making this community a great breeding ground for ideas! So I wanted to discuss the best points that have been raised thus far:

 

  • Mobilizing users to determine the quality of different journalists.
  • A ranking system should be established once that quality can be determined.
  • Using the system historians use to determine bias and falsehoods.
  • Trusted news sources should have an opportunity to be rewarded with whitelisting on Adblock, Ublock, etc.
  • Involving people with as many different view points as possible, so the process itself is not prone to bias.
  • We should group information by story, and add this to the UI as well.
  • Implement blockchain authentication for users on the eventual service itself for contributors.

 

These are all great suggestions, and I thank you all so much for helping with this! Implementing this model on every news story is impossible at the start, so I believe we should focus on one story to see how this can work in practice. My suggestion is to use the Snowden story for this test case. I am nominating this story, because I believe enough time has passed since the beginning of it. Therefore, we should have more than enough data on different journalists, to see who said what and how those claims held up in reality. That is in no way final, so any suggestions are welcome!

 

tl;dr: These are the suggestions I got from this post. I suggest working on the Snowden story, to see this model in action. Suggestions are welcome!

I walk into the French patisserie and order a double espresso and a custard gateau. I sit me down at one of the three small tables outside and wait for the waitress to deliver. She is French. I can tell from her accent. Young. Early twenties, I guess.

An elderly couple sit at the central table. 'Elderly' but younger than I am. As I sit down at one of the unoccupied tables the man says, "Good afternoon."

I am surprised but return the greeting. The woman says nothing.

The waitress brings my order and sets it down on the table. The man at the adjacent table says something but I can't hear him properly and I ask him to repeat it.

"Are there any other places here where one can get a coffee?" he says.

I am surprised for the second time. There is a Starbucks directly across the road, and a Costas immediately next to the patisserie. Both have a few outside tables and more inside.

"Yes," I say, and point them out to him.

"Oh," he says.

"About a hundred yards further down the road," I add, " there is a small Lebanese restaurant. You can get a good cup of coffee there too."

"Oh," he says again.

They are obviously strangers here but are not dressed as tourists and carry no luggage.

I get on with my custard gateau and coffee. In a little while the man and the woman rise. First the man and then the woman say "goodbye," and walk away. She is walking slowly and carefully but without assistance.

I am reflecting on the fact that I have spoken more words to these strangers than to anyone in the past week.

Why am I thinking of Longfellow's poem "Ships that pass in the night," I wonder.
